tip: Formal commands keep 'Sie' right after the verb: 'erzählen Sie uns'. The pronoun stays, unlike informal commands.
'Raten' (to advise) takes the person in the dative: 'ich rate dir' means I advise you.
A present passive plus a future time word reads as future: 'wird nächste Woche repariert' means will be repaired next week.
'Halb' counts toward the next hour, not past the last: 'halb neun' means 8:30, half an hour before nine.
'Sollen' can mean supposed to or reportedly: 'es soll regnen' means rain is expected, people say so.
In passives, name the doer with 'von' plus dative: 'von vielen Leuten besucht' means attended by many people.
The 'du' command of 'sein' is irregular: it is simply 'sei', as in 'sei nicht traurig'.
German keeps the present tense with 'seit' for ongoing actions: 'wird seit Monaten gebaut' means has been under construction for months.
The genitive shows possession and usually adds '-es' to short neuter nouns: 'des alten Hauses' means of the old house.
Reported speech uses a special verb form to flag a claim, not a fact: 'sie habe den Unfall nicht verursacht', with 'habe' instead of 'hat'.
German normally builds the passive with 'werden', not 'sein': 'wird das Essen frisch zubereitet' = the food is prepared fresh.
Motion verbs usually form the perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'sind wir den ganzen Tag gewandert' means we hiked all day.
'Hose' is singular in German though English pants is plural: 'eine bequeme Hose' means one pair.
'Bevor' is a linking word that sends the verb to the end: 'bevor du das Haus betrittst'.
'Wegen' means 'because of' and takes the genitive: 'wegen des Staus' = because of the traffic jam. Spoken German often uses the dative.
'Putzen' means to clean or scrub, as in 'sie putzt das ganze Haus'; it is also the verb for brushing teeth.
After a comparative like 'größer', standard German uses 'als', not 'wie': 'größer als München'.
'Während' (during) takes the genitive case: 'während der Dämmerung'.
With no article, the adjective takes the ending the article would carry: 'deutscher Wein' (masculine).
'Abfahren' is a separable verb, so the prefix 'ab' moves to the end: 'fahren Sie an der nächsten Kreuzung rechts ab'.
German often shows 'of' with the genitive rather than a separate word: 'die Schönheit der Landschaft'.
'Gut' is irregular in the superlative: 'gut', 'besser', 'best-', giving 'die beste Idee', never 'gutste'.
'Tragen' means both to wear (clothes) and to carry: 'trägt einen eleganten Mantel' means wears an elegant coat.
Nouns ending in '-chen' are neuter, so it stays 'das Mädchen' even though it means a girl.
To report what someone said, German shifts the verb to a reporting form: 'sein' becomes 'seien' in 'die Ergebnisse seien'.
After 'alles', 'etwas', and 'nichts', the linking word is 'was', not 'das': 'alles, was ich darüber weiß'.
'Für' always takes the accusative: 'für die Arbeit'.
'Unter' can take dative or accusative; for a fixed location it is dative: 'unter der Eiche'.
'Zu' plus 'dem' contracts to 'zum': 'zum Schloss' (to the palace).
After 'den' (accusative masculine), the adjective ends in '-en': 'den wunderschönen Sonnenuntergang'.
